Thanks for that: I always struggle with landscape-type shots, thinking as you suggest that I should be focusing on a specific item - The wooden mess at the foreground plus the smaller thing off to the right, plus the hilltop covered in mist, make it too busy? Any tips about how to shoot something like that?

Sure! I love landscapes and while I don't think I'm a master by any means I think I could give you some critique. I think the way the shot is it's too busy like you said. Theres too many things in the shot that seem like they might be the subject, but I'm not really sure which one it is. My eyes kidna bounce around the photo without resting on any specific point.

Two things that I think will help you out with landscape shots:

  1. When taking the photo ask yourself "what is the main subject here?" If you can't answer the question then try to change that.

  2. Having an obvious foreground/midground/background setup can help add a lot of depth to landscape shots. Here is a really beautiful example that illustrates what I mean. It's obvious in this shot that the flowers are the main subject, but theres also a nice midground and background in the photo as well. It all adds together along with the beautiful early morning light to create an amazing photo.

If I were to go back and retake your photo I would try and shoot it so that the mess of the woodpile in front was the foreground main subject, the power lines served as the midground and the mountains/heavy fog were the gackground. I probably would of gotten a little closer to the woodpile and put it a teeny bit closer to the center so it was more obvious it was supposed to be the subject. Also the foreground of the photo is a bit underexposed. I'd assume this is probably because of the huge dynamic range cause by the fog.

I tried to fix the underexposed part and think it definitely improves what you already have a good bit.

Sorry for the wall of text! Just trying to pass on some of what I've learned in my short time shooting landscapes. Overall this is a good effort! Keep working at improving and you'll be getting amazing shots in no time.

Also feel free to stop by /v/photocritique for future critiques. We'd love to have you! :D
